title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
authors: John Zaris, Wes Johnson, Krishna Balaji Sogathur, Athreya Shankar, John J. Bollinger, Allison L. Carter, Murray J. Holland, Scott E. Parker
abstract: Motional modes of trapped-ion crystals in Penning traps can now be cooled to near their ground states via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. Numerical simulations are valuable tools for interpreting EIT cooling results and optimizing experimental protocols, but existing molecular dynamics codes are limited to the simulation of Doppler cooling. In this work, we fill this gap by implementing a semiclassical model of EIT cooling in a novel MD code. By simultaneously evolving the ions' internal quantum states and classical motion, we are able to calculate the instantaneous EIT laser forces acting on the ions. We first validate our code by comparing the single-ion cooling rate to fully quantum simulation results. Next, we analyze cooling of the drumhead modes in planar ion crystals, quantifying the effects of planar ion motion and a finite laser beam width. Finally, we demonstrate efficient EIT cooling of the axial modes in 3D ellipsoidal crystals containing up to 500 ions. Such crystals are a promising platform for future quantum sensing experiments with enhanced sensitivity. We find that the mode spectra of 3D crystals can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of the low-frequency $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. This numerical framework provides a powerful tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques and for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.
summary: This paper introduces a novel semiclassical molecular dynamics code to simulate Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) cooling in trapped-ion crystals. By coupling classical ion motion with internal quantum state evolution, the authors successfully model cooling in complex 2D and 3D geometries. This framework is a powerful tool for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information protocols.
main_problem: To develop and apply a semiclassical molecular dynamics simulation tool capable of modeling Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) cooling in ion crystals, extending beyond existing codes limited to Doppler cooling.
main_result: The framework successfully models efficient EIT cooling of axial modes in large 3D ion crystals, demonstrating that the mode spectra can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of low-frequency E x B modes.
method: The authors implemented a novel semiclassical MD code that simultaneously evolves the ions' classical motion and their internal quantum states, allowing for the calculation of instantaneous EIT laser forces.
model_or_system: The system involves trapped-ion crystals (2D and 3D) confined in a Penning trap. The cooling mechanism relies on EIT, which utilizes a $\Lambda$ level configuration, and the dynamics are governed by coupled classical equations of motion and quantum master equations.
key_observables: Instantaneous EIT laser forces, cooling rates, and the mode spectra of 3D crystals.
important_parameters: The simulation handles up to 500 ions, and the analysis focuses on sub-Doppler cooling regimes.
main_assumptions: The model uses a semiclassical approximation, which is noted to be less accurate when spontaneous emission recoil becomes significant.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Penning trap setup with both Doppler and EIT beams, the $\Lambda$ level structure for EIT, and show the cooling dynamics and mode spectra for 2D and 3D crystals.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for the new MD code, validates it by comparing single-ion cooling rates to quantum results, analyzes planar (2D) crystal cooling, and culminates in demonstrating efficient EIT cooling and mode engineering in 3D ellipsoidal crystals.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, advanced numerical tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques in complex, multi-ion quantum systems, directly impacting the feasibility of quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.
